body:
Drainage pattern of Gujarat

A drainage basin is the entire area from which a river and its tributaries collect water. Gujarat contains rivers originating outside the state, rivers originating within its uplands and rivers draining into inland depressions.

Most of Gujarat's principal rivers ultimately drain towards the Arabian Sea. However, some rivers of northern Gujarat terminate in the saline lowlands of the Rann rather than reaching the open sea through a clearly defined river mouth.

The four major mainland rivers

The Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada and Tapi are the principal rivers entering the Gujarat mainland from adjoining states. Their lower courses reach the Gulf of Khambhat and its adjoining Arabian Sea waters.

RiverOriginImportant location in Gujarat
SabarmatiAravalli Hills, RajasthanGandhinagar and Ahmedabad
MahiVindhyan uplands, Madhya PradeshMahisagar and lower central Gujarat
NarmadaAmarkantak, Madhya PradeshNarmada district and Bharuch
TapiMultai, Betul district, Madhya PradeshTapi district and Surat

Sabarmati

The Sabarmati rises in the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan and flows through northern and central Gujarat before reaching the Gulf of Khambhat. Gandhinagar and Ahmedabad are located along this river.

Its important tributaries include the Hathmati, Harnav, Watrak and Meshwo rivers. Water from the river system is used for irrigation and urban water supply.

Mahi

The Mahi originates in Madhya Pradesh, passes through Rajasthan and enters Gujarat before reaching the Gulf of Khambhat. Its course is therefore associated with 3 states.

The Panam is an important tributary of the Mahi. The Mahi basin contains major irrigation and reservoir projects, including Kadana and the Panam project.

Narmada

The Narmada rises at Amarkantak and flows westward through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura systems. It enters Gujarat in the eastern uplands and reaches the Gulf of Khambhat through an estuary near Bharuch.

An estuary is a coastal river mouth where river water mixes with seawater under tidal influence. Unlike a large depositional delta, an estuary commonly has a broad tidal opening.

The Karjan and Orsang are important tributaries of the Narmada in Gujarat. The Sardar Sarovar Dam is constructed on the Narmada.

Tapi

The Tapi, also called the Tapti, originates near Multai in Madhya Pradesh. It flows westward through Maharashtra and enters Gujarat. Its lower course passes through Surat and reaches the Arabian Sea near Hazira, at the southern opening of the Gulf of Khambhat.

Like the Narmada, the Tapi flows westward through a rift valley and forms an estuary. The Ukai Dam is an important multipurpose project on the Tapi.

From north to south, the principal river mouths along the Gulf of Khambhat and its southern opening are the Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada and Tapi.

Rivers of northern Gujarat

The West Banas, Saraswati and Rupen are important rivers associated with the inland and saline drainage areas of northern Gujarat.

  • West Banas: Originates in the Aravalli region of Rajasthan, flows through northern Gujarat and reaches the Little Rann of Kachchh.
  • Saraswati: Flows through the northern Gujarat plains, including the Sidhpur–Patan region, towards the Rann lowlands.
  • Rupen: Drains part of northern Gujarat towards the Little Rann.

The West Banas must be distinguished from the Banas River of Rajasthan that joins the Chambal River. They belong to different drainage systems.

Rivers of Saurashtra

Many Saurashtra rivers originate in the interior uplands and flow outward towards different coastal sectors. This produces a broadly radial drainage arrangement.

RiverGeneral drainage direction
BhadarWest and south-west towards the Arabian Sea
OzatWest towards the Arabian Sea
ShetrunjiEast towards the Gulf of Khambhat
AjiNorth towards the Gulf of Kachchh
MachhuNorth towards the Little Rann region

Rivers of South Gujarat

South Gujarat contains several shorter west-flowing rivers that collect rainfall from the eastern hills and cross the coastal plains.

The Purna, Ambika, Auranga, Par, Kolak and Damanganga are important examples. Many of these rivers receive substantial monsoon runoff from the southern hill tracts. The Damanganga also flows through Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman before reaching the Arabian Sea.

Prelims focus

  • Sabarmati originates in the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan.
  • Mahi flows through Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • Narmada originates at Amarkantak; Tapi at Multai.
  • Narmada and Tapi are west-flowing rift-valley rivers forming estuaries.
  • West Banas and Rupen drain towards the Little Rann.
  • Trap: Shetrunji flows generally eastward within Saurashtra, whereas Bhadar flows generally westward.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 3, Drainage, section on Peninsular Rivers; Central Water Commission and ISRO, River Basin Atlas of India, 2012, Sabarmati, Mahi, Narmada, Tapi and Kutch–Saurashtra basin maps; Central Ground Water Board, Report on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of Gujarat State as on March 2022, Section 1.3, Drainage; Gujarat Ecology Commission, Rivers of Gujarat, 11 June 2014; Survey of India, Gujarat State Map, 2026; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Understanding dams and reservoirs

A dam is a barrier constructed across a river to regulate or store water. The water body formed behind it is called a reservoir. A multipurpose river project may provide irrigation, drinking water, hydroelectricity and flood regulation.

A dam must be identified by the river on which it is constructed, not merely by the nearest city or the region that receives its water. A canal may transfer stored water from one river basin to another without changing the natural drainage direction of the river.

Major mainland river projects

ProjectRiverLocation
Sardar SarovarNarmadaEkta Nagar–Navagam, Narmada district
UkaiTapiTapi district
KakraparTapiSurat district
KadanaMahiMahisagar district
WanakboriMahiLower Mahi, Central Gujarat
DharoiSabarmatiMehsana–Sabarkantha region
DantiwadaWest BanasBanaskantha district
PanamPanamPanchmahal district
KarjanKarjanNarmada district
MadhubanDamangangaSouthern Gujarat border region

Sardar Sarovar Project

The Sardar Sarovar Dam is a major multipurpose project on the Narmada River. It is situated in eastern Gujarat near Navagam and Ekta Nagar, formerly known as Kevadia.

The project supplies irrigation and drinking water through an extensive canal network. The Narmada Main Canal carries water towards water-deficient areas of northern and western Gujarat, with distribution through branch canals to regions including Saurashtra and Kachchh.

The project illustrates the distinction between a natural river basin and an artificially constructed irrigation network. Narmada water reaches Kachchh through canal infrastructure, but the natural course of the Narmada continues towards the Gulf of Khambhat.

Ukai and Kakrapar

Both projects are situated on the Tapi River. Ukai is a major storage dam with a reservoir known as Vallabh Sagar. Kakrapar is a downstream weir used for diversion and regulation of river water.

A weir is a barrier across a river that raises or regulates the water level, often to divert water into canals. It need not create a reservoir comparable in size to that of a major storage dam.

Kadana and Wanakbori

Kadana is a storage and hydroelectric project on the Mahi River. Wanakbori is a downstream weir on the same river. The two projects must be associated with the Mahi rather than the Narmada or Tapi.

Dharoi and Dantiwada

Dharoi is constructed on the Sabarmati, whereas Dantiwada is constructed on the West Banas. Both projects serve the relatively water-deficient northern Gujarat region but belong to separate river systems.

Important projects in Saurashtra

ProjectRiverAssociated area
Bhadar DamBhadarRajkot district
Aji DamAjiRajkot
Machhu-II DamMachhuMorbi
Shetrunji DamShetrunjiPalitana region, Bhavnagar district

Projects on tributaries

The Panam Dam is situated on the Panam River, which is a tributary of the Mahi. The Karjan Dam is situated on the Karjan River, which is a tributary of the Narmada.

These examples illustrate the difference between a project on the main river and a project within its wider basin. The Karjan project belongs to the Narmada basin but is not constructed across the main Narmada River.

Prelims focus

  • Sardar Sarovar–Narmada; Ukai–Tapi.
  • Kadana and Wanakbori–Mahi.
  • Dharoi–Sabarmati; Dantiwada–West Banas.
  • Machhu-II–Machhu River, Morbi.
  • Panam belongs to the Mahi basin; Karjan belongs to the Narmada basin.
  • Trap: The Narmada Main Canal is an artificial water-transfer channel, not a natural branch of the Narmada River.

[Sources: Government of Gujarat, Narmada, Water Resources, Water Supply and Kalpsar Department, Disaster Management Plan 2021–22, reservoir and flood information tables; Gujarat Water Resources Department, Administrative Report 2009–10, major irrigation schemes; Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Limited, Sardar Sarovar Project and canal system information; Survey of India, Gujarat State Map, 2026; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Coastal geography

Gujarat's coastline includes open Arabian Sea shores, gulfs, tidal creeks, estuaries, mangroves and extensive intertidal mudflats. These features strongly influence the location and development of ports.

A gulf is a large extension of seawater penetrating into the land. Gujarat contains 2 major gulfs: the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat.

FeatureGulf of KachchhGulf of Khambhat
PositionBetween Kachchh and northern SaurashtraBetween eastern Saurashtra and mainland Gujarat
General orientationWest to eastSouth to north
Important coastal featuresCoral reefs, islands, mangroves and creeksEstuaries, mudflats and strong tidal influence
Examples of portsKandla, Mundra, Sikka, NavlakhiBhavnagar, Dahej

Major and non-major ports

The classification of Indian ports into major and non-major ports is administrative. It does not depend solely on the amount of cargo handled, physical size or commercial importance.

Deendayal Port, formerly known as Kandla Port, is Gujarat's only centrally administered major port in the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways report for April–September 2025–26.

The report identifies 49 ports in Gujarat, consisting of 1 major port and 48 non-major ports. These figures describe that reporting period and include ports with different levels of commercial activity.

Mundra is a large commercial port but belongs to the non-major port category. Gujarat Maritime Board is the principal state maritime authority associated with the development and administration of the state's non-major port sector.

A large cargo-handling port can be classified as a non-major port. The term major port represents a legal and administrative category rather than a simple ranking by size.

Ports of Kachchh and the Gulf of Kachchh

PortDistrictCoastal location
JakhauKachchhWestern Kachchh coast
MandviKachchhSouthern Kachchh coast
MundraKachchhNorthern side of Gulf of Kachchh
Deendayal Port, KandlaKachchhInner northern Gulf of Kachchh
NavlakhiMorbiInner eastern end of Gulf of Kachchh
BediJamnagarSouthern side of Gulf of Kachchh
SikkaJamnagarSouthern side of Gulf of Kachchh
VadinarDevbhumi DwarkaSouthern side of Gulf of Kachchh
OkhaDevbhumi DwarkaWestern entrance of Gulf of Kachchh

Ports of southern and eastern Saurashtra

PortDistrict
PorbandarPorbandar
VeravalGir Somnath
JafrabadAmreli
PipavavAmreli
MahuvaBhavnagar
BhavnagarBhavnagar

Veraval is an important fishing and coastal commercial centre. Pipavav is associated with maritime cargo transport. Bhavnagar is located near the western side of the Gulf of Khambhat.

Alang, in Bhavnagar district, is internationally known for ship recycling. Its broad tidal shore and considerable tidal variation are geographical factors associated with the development of this activity.

Ports of mainland Gujarat

PortDistrictGeographical association
DahejBharuchEastern Gulf of Khambhat
HaziraSuratCoast near the Tapi estuary
MagdallaSuratLower Tapi River
BillimoraNavsariSouth Gujarat coastal region

Dahej and Hazira are closely associated with industrial activity and the movement of bulk cargo and energy resources. Their locations illustrate how port development may support nearby industrial regions.

Geographical sequence along the coast

Along the outer Saurashtra coast, the general sequence from the western tip towards the Gulf of Khambhat is Okha, Porbandar, Veraval, Jafrabad, Pipavav, Mahuva, Alang and Bhavnagar.

On the mainland side, Dahej lies north of the Surat-area ports of Hazira and Magdalla. Identifying which side of a gulf a port occupies is often more useful than remembering its name alone.

Prelims focus

  • Deendayal Port is the renamed Kandla Port.
  • Kandla and Mundra are located in Kachchh.
  • Navlakhi is associated with Morbi district and the inner Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Pipavav is in Amreli; Dahej is in Bharuch; Hazira is in Surat.
  • Alang in Bhavnagar district is a ship-recycling centre.
  • Trap: Mundra is classified as a non-major port despite its commercial importance.

[Sources: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Update on the Indian Ports Sector, April–September 2025–26, Section 2.2.1, Gujarat, Figure 10 and p. 14; Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, parliamentary information on operational Other Than Major Ports, 2026, Gujarat list; Gujarat Maritime Board, port sector information; Survey of India, Gujarat State Map, 2026; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
